questions.stem: A card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52 cards. What is the probability it is a king?

options.option_text: 1/52 (probability of one specific card — not any king)
1/4 (probability of a suit — not specific rank)

questions.explanation: A is correct. There are 4 kings in a deck of 52 cards. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. Deck structure: 52 cards = 4 suits × 13 ranks. Each rank (A,2,...,K) has exactly 4 cards (one per suit).

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red balls, 4 blue balls, and 5 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability of drawing a blue ball?

options.option_text: 1/3 (wrong: 4/12=1/3 is actually correct — let me re-check: 4/12=1/3 ✓)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Total balls = 3+4+5 = 12. P(blue) = 4/12 = 1/3.

questions.stem: Two dice are thrown simultaneously. What is the probability of getting a sum of 7?

options.option_text: 1/6 (correct: pairs giving sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs; total outcomes=36; P=6/36=1/6 ✓)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Pairs summing to 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs. P(sum=7) = 6/36 = 1/6. Useful table: sum=7 has the most ways (6) of any sum — it's the most likely total on two dice.

questions.stem: A coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?

options.option_text: 3/8 (correct: outcomes with exactly 2 heads: HHT, HTH, THH = 3; total outcomes=2³=8; P=3/8 ✓)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Total outcomes = 2³ = 8. Favourable (exactly 2 heads): HHT, HTH, THH = 3. P = 3/8. Alternative: ³C₂ × (1/2)² × (1/2)¹ = 3 × 1/4 × 1/2 = 3/8. Binomial formula confirms.

questions.stem: From a group of 4 men and 3 women, 2 people are selected at random. What is the probability that both are women?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Total ways to choose 2 from 7 = ⁷C₂ = 21. Ways to choose 2 women from 3 = ³C₂ = 3. P(both women) = 3/21 = 1/7.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a deck of 52. What is the probability of getting a red face card?

options.option_text: 3/26 (correct: red face cards=6 (3 per suit × 2 red suits); P=6/52=3/26 ✓)
1/13 (4/52 — that's probability of any face card of one suit)
1/4 (probability of red card = 1/2; face card = 12/52; these are not addable directly)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Face cards = J, Q, K = 3 per suit × 4 suits = 12. Red face cards = 3 (hearts) + 3 (diamonds) = 6. P = 6/52 = 3/26. Remember: face cards = J, Q, K (not Ace); red suits = hearts + diamonds.

questions.stem: Events A and B are mutually exclusive. P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(A or B)?

options.option_text: 0.12 (P(A)×P(B) = 0.4×0.3 = 0.12 — that's P(A and B) for independent events)
0.58 (P(A)+P(B)−P(A)×P(B) = 0.4+0.3−0.12 — formula for independent, not mutually exclusive)
1.0 (wrong: probabilities don't sum to 1 unless complementary)

questions.explanation: B is correct. For mutually exclusive events (cannot occur simultaneously): P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B) = 0.4+0.3 = 0.7. For non-mutually exclusive: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Mutually exclusive means P(A∩B) = 0.

questions.stem: A bag has 6 white and 4 black balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are white?
questions.explanation: B is correct. P(first white) = 6/10. P(second white | first was white) = 5/9 (5 white remain, 9 total remain). P(both white) = 6/10 × 5/9 = 30/90 = 1/3. Alternative: ⁶C₂/¹⁰C₂ = 15/45 = 1/3 ✓. Key: without replacement changes the second draw's probability.

questions.stem: What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4 when a die is rolled?

options.option_text: 2/3 (P(4 or more) = 3/6 = 1/2 — but question says GREATER than 4)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Die outcomes: {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Greater than 4: {5,6} = 2 outcomes. P = 2/6 = 1/3. Trap: 'greater than 4' does NOT include 4 itself. Compare: P(≥4) = 3/6 = 1/2; P(>4) = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.stem: The probability that it rains on a day is 0.3. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?

options.option_text: Cannot determine (complement rule makes it deterministic)

questions.explanation: B is correct. P(event) + P(complement) = 1. P(no rain) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. Complement rule is one of the most used tools in probability: P(Ā) = 1 − P(A).

questions.stem: Two students A and B appear for an interview. P(A is selected) = 1/3 and P(B is selected) = 1/5. Assuming selections are independent, what is the probability that exactly one of them is selected?
questions.explanation: B is correct. P(exactly one selected) = P(A selected, B not) + P(A not, B selected). = (1/3)×(4/5) + (2/3)×(1/5) = 4/15 + 2/15 = 6/15 = 2/5. Verify: P(none) = (2/3)(4/5) = 8/15; P(both) = (1/3)(1/5) = 1/15; P(exactly one) = 1−8/15−1/15 = 6/15 = 2/5 ✓.

questions.stem: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 20. What is the probability it is divisible by both 2 and 3?

options.option_text: 1/10 (wrong: numbers divisible by 6 in 1-20: 6,12,18=3 numbers; P=3/20 not 1/10=2/20)
3/20 (correct: divisible by both 2 and 3 = divisible by LCM(2,3)=6; multiples of 6 in 1-20: 6,12,18; P=3/20 ✓)
1/3 (wrong — but close: multiples of 3 in 1-20 = 6, so 6/20=3/10)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Divisible by both 2 and 3 means divisible by LCM(2,3) = 6. Multiples of 6 in {1,...,20}: 6, 12, 18 → 3 numbers. P = 3/20. Key: 'divisible by both a and b' → use LCM, not just multiplication.
